html:
The landing of the Dutch navigator Willem Janszoon and his crew on the west coast of Cape York Peninsula, in the far north of Australia, in early 1606. It is the first known landing by Europeans on the continent.

Janszoon sailed the small ship Duyfken from Bantam for the Dutch East India Company, looking for trade along the coast of New Guinea. He sailed south from New Guinea into the Gulf of Carpentaria and charted some 300 km of coast, thinking it was part of New Guinea. His men went ashore several times; there were clashes with local Aboriginal people, and some of the crew were killed. He reported the land as swampy and poor.

A few months later the Spanish captain Luis Váez de Torres sailed through the strait that now bears his name, proving there was water between New Guinea and Australia, though this stayed little known. More Dutch ships touched the west coast over the next decades, and Abel Tasman mapped more in 1642 and 1644. Long before any European, Makassan fishermen were visiting the north coast.
